name: The Kelly–Hopkinsville encounter
coord_source: Wikipedia: Kelly, Kentucky (community coordinates; the Sutton farmhouse stood nearby)
beings: Witnesses described several small figures about 3 to 3.5 feet tall with large round heads, big pointed ears, long arms ending in claw-like hands, glowing yellowish eyes and a shiny, metallic-looking body; some said they seemed to float.
witnesses: Nearly a dozen people at the Sutton farmhouse, adults and children; the adults most often named are Glennie Lankford, Elmer "Lucky" Sutton and Billy Ray Taylor.
summary: A Kentucky farm family said small glowing-eyed creatures besieged their house for hours and shrugged off gunfire.
body: On the evening of Sunday, August 21, 1955, Billy Ray Taylor, a visitor at the Sutton family farmhouse near the hamlet of Kelly, said he saw a bright object streak across the sky and come down beyond the trees while he was drawing water from the well. The household laughed it off. About an hour later the family dog started barking, and Taylor and Elmer "Lucky" Sutton said they saw a small glowing figure approaching the back door. They fired at it with a shotgun and a .22 rifle; the figure flipped over and ran into the dark.

According to the family, more of the creatures then appeared at windows, on the roof and in a tree, and the men kept shooting. They said the bullets seemed to have no effect and sounded as if they were hitting metal. When Taylor stepped outside, a clawed hand reportedly touched his hair from the roof overhang. After several hours of hiding inside, the group fled in their cars at about 11 p.m. to the Hopkinsville police station; one investigator measured a witness's pulse at 140 beats a minute. Matriarch Glennie Lankford later said she had seen one of the figures herself, shining like metal.

Police chief Russell Greenwell called for backup, and city police, Kentucky state troopers, Christian County deputies and military police from Fort Campbell went to the farm, along with a Kentucky New Era photographer. They found spent shell casings, a broken window and holes in the screens, but no tracks, blood or landing marks, and reported no sign that anyone had been drinking. After the officers left, the family said the creatures came back in the early hours of the morning. The next day the house was empty; neighbours said the family had packed up and left. Sightseers soon swarmed the farm, and the family began charging admission, which led critics to call them fortune seekers.

Explanations have ranged widely. Project Blue Book listed the case as a hoax without further comment, though it does not appear to have investigated beyond contacting Fort Campbell personnel. Researcher Isabel Davis, who investigated in 1956 and later co-wrote a long report with Ted Bloecher, found the hoax and hallucination theories unconvincing. Skeptic Joe Nickell argued that the family met aggressive great horned owls, which are about two feet tall, have yellow eyes and ear tufts, fly silently and defend their nests, and that Taylor's light was a meteor. Others have suggested excitement or drink played a part. None of these explanations has been confirmed.

The case gave popular culture the term "little green men", although the witnesses never said the beings were green; reporters added the colour later. It became known as the Hopkinsville Goblins case, inspired Steven Spielberg's unmade film Night Skies and loosely the 1986 film Critters, and is celebrated each year at Kelly's Little Green Men Days festival.
status_note: Blue Book called it a hoax and skeptics favour owls, but no hoax has been shown and the witness accounts were consistent.

official.note: The family reported the attack at the police station on the night of August 21, 1955; Chief Russell Greenwell led the response.

official.agency: Kentucky State Police and Christian County Sheriff's Office
official.note: State troopers and sheriff's deputies joined the overnight search of the farm and found no evidence of the creatures.
Military police from Fort Campbell accompanied local officers to the farmhouse.

official.agency: US Air Force, Project Blue Book
official.note: Blue Book listed the case as a hoax; no investigation file was found in the digitised Blue Book folders.

name: The Flatwoods monster
place: Flatwoods, Braxton County, West Virginia, USA
beings: Witnesses described a figure around 10 feet tall with a round, red face inside a pointed, hood-like shape, glowing eyes, a dark body with folds like clothing and, in some accounts, small claw-like hands.
witnesses: Seven people: local mother Kathleen May, National Guardsman Eugene Lemon and several local boys.
summary: After a light fell from the sky, a group in Flatwoods said a towering, hooded figure with a glowing face hissed and glided toward them.
body: At about 7:15 p.m. on September 12, 1952, several boys in Flatwoods said they saw a bright object cross the sky and come down on a farm on a nearby hill. They fetched Kathleen May, the mother of two of the boys, and a group of seven, including West Virginia National Guardsman Eugene Lemon, climbed the hill to look. Near the top they reported a pulsating red light. When Lemon pointed his flashlight toward it, the group said it lit up a tall, man-like figure with a round red face inside a pointed hood.

In interviews recorded by writer Gray Barker, the witnesses said the figure was about 10 feet tall, made a hissing sound and glided toward them. Lemon dropped his flashlight and everyone ran. Several said they smelled a stinging mist; some later felt sick, and a doctor was called to examine the boys, but no cause was found. The local sheriff and a deputy searched the site that night and reported they saw, heard and smelled nothing. The next day a local newspaperman said he found skid marks and a gummy residue in the field, which UFO groups later cited as landing traces.

The US Air Force's Project Blue Book record card for Flatwoods concludes that the object was the well-known meteor that crossed Maryland, Pennsylvania and West Virginia that evening, calling the case "the West Virginia monster so called". In 2000 skeptic Joe Nickell visited the area and argued that the red light was an aircraft beacon and the "monster" a startled barn owl on a tree limb, with foliage below it forming the "skirt" and its talons the claw-like hands. A local teenager later said he had driven his truck around the site, which may explain the tracks.

The case was national news in 1952. Today Flatwoods calls itself home of the Green Monster, the Flatwoods Monster Museum operates in nearby Sutton, Braxton County has placed giant monster-shaped chairs around the area, and the town has held a Flatwoods Monster convention since 2019. The 2019 TV drama Project Blue Book dramatised the story.
status_note: The Air Force explained the light as a meteor and skeptics propose an owl, but the witnesses never accepted that explanation.

official.note: The sheriff and a deputy searched the hilltop the same night and found nothing unusual.

official.agency: US Air Force, Project Blue Book
official.note: The Blue Book record card for Flatwoods concludes the object was the meteor of September 12, 1952.

sources.title: Flatwoods Monster (e-WV: The West Virginia Encyclopedia)

name: The Valensole encounter
beings: The farmer described two small figures, about the size of eight-year-old children, in one-piece suits, with large, pumpkin-shaped heads and a mouth like a simple opening.
witnesses: One witness, lavender farmer Maurice Masse.
summary: A Provence lavender farmer said two small beings by an egg-shaped craft froze him in place with a tube-like device.
body: Early on the morning of July 1, 1965, lavender farmer Maurice Masse was starting work in his field near Valensole, on the Valensole plateau in Provence, when he said he heard a whistling sound. He then saw an egg-shaped object, about the size of a small car, resting on legs among the lavender, with two small figures beside it.

Masse said one of the beings pointed a tube-like device at him and he found himself unable to move. He watched them, he said, looking at the plants and making grunting sounds, before they climbed back into the craft, which rose and flew off. He remained paralysed for some time afterwards. He later told his wife he had felt some kind of communication from them, and he treated the spot as special for the rest of his life.

The Gendarmerie investigated. Investigators and the press recorded marks in the soil, including a central hole, which Masse said hardened like cement; within days, sightseers had trampled the site. Neighbours and family described him as a private man with no interest in fame, and researcher Jacques Vallée, who also looked into the case, considered it unexplained. France's official UFO office, GEIPAN, never carried out its own study, but in 2015, for the 50th anniversary, it released the three Gendarmerie reports, which it considers the most reliable documents on the case.

A passing military helicopter was suggested at the time; Masse rejected that idea, and French skeptics have argued that he made up the story and the traces. No explanation has been confirmed, and Valensole remains one of the best-known entity cases in Europe.
status_note: No explanation has been confirmed; GEIPAN released the Gendarmerie reports but published no conclusion of its own.

official.note: Gendarmes investigated the reported landing in July 1965 and filed three reports.
Published the three Gendarmerie reports in 2015 without classifying the case as explained.

sources.title: Le cas toujours « inexpliqué » de Valensole (Futura Sciences)

name: The Pascagoula abduction
beings: Charles Hickson described three creatures with pincer-like hands who took hold of the two men and floated them aboard the craft.
witnesses: Two men, Charles Hickson and his younger companion Calvin Parker.
summary: Two men fishing on the Pascagoula River said creatures with pincers floated them into a craft and examined them.
body: On the evening of October 11, 1973, Charles Hickson and his younger companion Calvin Parker were fishing from a pier on the west bank of the Pascagoula River in Mississippi. They said they heard a whirring sound, saw flashing blue lights and then an oval object about 30 to 40 feet across. According to Hickson, three creatures with pincer-like hands came out, took hold of them and floated them aboard, where Hickson said he was examined. Parker, he said, fainted and was unconscious for most of it. The men said they were then returned to the riverbank.

Around 11 p.m. the pair went to the Jackson County sheriff's office. Captain Glenn Ryder said he first suspected a prank, so officers left the two alone in a room with a hidden tape recorder; their private conversation matched what they had said, and Ryder came to believe they were sincere. The next day they were checked for radiation at Keesler Air Force Base and released. Astronomer J. Allen Hynek and ufologist James Harder interviewed them under hypnosis and told the press they believed the men had experienced something real. A local polygraph examiner later said Hickson believed what he described.

Skeptic Philip J. Klass pointed to inconsistencies in Hickson's account and his refusal of a polygraph by a more experienced examiner, and concluded it was a hoax. Joe Nickell suggested Hickson may have had a vivid waking dream and that Parker, who said he had blacked out, went along with it. Hickson later claimed further contacts with the beings, which critics saw as embellishment.

Both men stood by their account for life. Hickson died in 2011; Parker published his own book in 2018 and died in 2023. In 2019 the local historical society unveiled a historical marker near the site, and Pascagoula now holds an annual festival marking the anniversary.
status_note: Police found the men sincere, while skeptics suspect a hoax or a waking dream; neither has been shown.

official.note: Took the men's report on the night of October 11, 1973, and secretly recorded them; officers said their story stayed consistent.

official.agency: US Air Force, Keesler Air Force Base
official.note: The two men were examined at Keesler AFB the next day and cleared of radiation exposure.

sources.title: Historical marker commemorates reported alien abduction (AP, via Las Vegas Review-Journal)

name: The Varginha incident
beings: Three young women described a crouching, unsteady creature with a large head bearing three bumps, vein-like markings on its skin and eyes like two red balls.
witnesses: Three young women aged 14 to 22, followed by many second-hand claims from other residents.
summary: Three young women in Varginha said they saw a crouching creature with red eyes, sparking rumours of a captured alien.
body: At about 3:30 p.m. on January 20, 1996, three young women walking through the Jardim Andere neighbourhood of Varginha, in Minas Gerais, said they saw a strange being crouched by a wall on a vacant lot. They described a large-headed figure with three bumps on its head, veined skin and red eyes, which looked weak or injured. Frightened, they ran home and told their mother they had seen the devil.

The story spread quickly. Over the following months, residents and ufologists made a series of further claims: that UFOs had been seen in the days before, that the army and fire service had captured one or more creatures and taken them to hospitals and then to Campinas, that a police officer had died after handling one, and that several animals at the local zoo had died mysteriously. Ufologists linked these reports into a single story of a crash and a cover-up.

The Brazilian Army opened a military police inquiry (IPM) in 1996. It concluded that the women had most likely seen a local man known as "Mudinho", who probably had a mental disability, and who may have been dirty from heavy rain and crouching by a wall. It said the military trucks and personnel seen that day were on routine duties, such as vehicle maintenance, that had been misread as a capture operation. Brazil's Superior Military Court later made the inquiry's two volumes available online. Ufologists, including the main local investigators, reject that explanation, noting that the women would have known the man.

Varginha has embraced the story: the town has alien-themed bus shelters, a flying-saucer-shaped water tower and souvenirs of the "ET de Varginha". The case has been the subject of many Brazilian books, a 2022 documentary, Moment of Contact, and a 2025 Brazilian documentary.
status_note: A Brazilian Army inquiry attributed the sighting to a local man, but ufologists reject this and claim a cover-up.

official.note: Opened in 1996; concluded the women saw a local man and that troop movements were routine.
Made the two volumes of the military inquiry publicly available online.

sources.title: Caso de ET de Varginha faz 30 anos: saiba o que investigação mostrou (IstoÉ)

name: The Kecksburg incident
beings: No beings appear in the contemporary record; witnesses described a fireball and, in later accounts, an acorn-shaped object in the woods. It is included here as a landmark object case, not an entity sighting.
witnesses: Residents of Kecksburg and observers across several states and Ontario who saw the fireball.
summary: A fireball seen over six states was said to have come down in woods near Kecksburg, Pennsylvania; no beings were reported.
body: Important caveat: Kecksburg is an object case. No witness in the 1965 record described beings or occupants. It is included in this section because of its fame as "Pennsylvania's Roswell", and the entry sticks to what people actually reported.

At about 4:44 p.m. on December 9, 1965, a brilliant fireball crossed the sky over the Detroit–Windsor area and was seen from at least six US states and Ontario. Pilots made reports, sonic booms were heard, and small grass fires were blamed on it. In the village of Kecksburg, about 30 miles southeast of Pittsburgh, some residents said they heard a thump, saw blue smoke and believed something had come down in the woods.

The Greensburg Tribune-Review reported that the area was sealed off by state police and army officials awaiting experts. State troopers and Air Force personnel searched the woods and said they found nothing, and the paper's next edition ran the headline "Searchers fail to find object". Astronomers and the Department of Defense said the fireball was most likely a meteor. Project Blue Book filed the event under the multi-state fireball of that date and concluded it was a meteor. A 1967 scientific study using photographs and seismograph data put the fireball's end over western Lake Erie, far from Kecksburg.

Years later, some residents said they had seen a bronze, acorn-shaped object the size of a car, with markings like hieroglyphs, being taken away on a flatbed truck. In 2005 NASA said experts had once examined fragments and found them to be from a Soviet satellite, but that the records had been lost; after a Freedom of Information lawsuit, NASA agreed in 2007 under a court order to search again, and testified that boxes of papers from the period were missing. NASA's own satellite data, however, rule out the Soviet probe Kosmos 96, and the meteor explanation remains the mainstream view.
The case was featured on Unsolved Mysteries in 1990, and the acorn-shaped prop built for the show is still displayed in the village.
status_note: Scientists and the Air Force identified a meteor; later witness claims of a recovered object are unconfirmed.

official.note: Troopers cordoned off and searched the woods on December 9, 1965, and reported finding nothing.

official.agency: US Air Force, Project Blue Book
official.note: Filed the December 9, 1965 fireball (Indiana, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Canada) as a meteor.
Said in 2005 that fragments had been identified as Soviet satellite debris but the records were lost; searched for records under a 2007 court order.

sources.title: Project Blue Book: December 9, 1965 fireball (National Archives)

name: The Socorro landing (Lonnie Zamora)
beings: Zamora briefly saw two figures in white coveralls beside the object, normal in shape but small, like small adults or large children.
witnesses: One main witness, Socorro police sergeant Lonnie Zamora; other officers saw the ground marks afterwards.
summary: A Socorro police sergeant said he saw two small figures in white beside a shiny egg-shaped object that roared off in a flame.
body: At about 5:45 p.m. on April 24, 1964, Socorro police sergeant Lonnie Zamora was chasing a speeding car south of town when he heard a roar and saw a flame in the sky to the southwest. Thinking a dynamite shack might have exploded, he left the chase to check. In a gully he saw a shiny, whitish object shaped like an "O" that he first took for an overturned car, and briefly saw two figures in white coveralls standing beside it.

As Zamora drove closer, he said he heard a loud roar and saw a blue and orange flame under the object, which rose and moved quickly away. He radioed for help, and New Mexico State Police Sergeant Chavez arrived soon after. Officers found burning and smouldering brush and shallow depressions in the ground where Zamora said the object had stood.

The US Air Force's Project Blue Book investigated, and the case fills one of the larger Blue Book folders, at about 170 pages. Blue Book could not identify the object and listed the case as "unknown", one of its best-known unsolved landing reports.

Proposed explanations include a test of a lunar landing craft from White Sands Missile Range, a hoax by New Mexico Tech students (an idea supported by the college's then-president Stirling Colgate), a mirage of the star Canopus, and, from skeptic Philip J. Klass, a scheme to boost tourism. None has been proven. Zamora died in Socorro in 2009. The town built a viewing area near the site and in 2012 commissioned a mural marking the event.
status_note: Project Blue Book listed the case as unknown, and later hoax and test-craft theories remain unproven.

official.note: Sgt. Lonnie Zamora reported the sighting by radio while on duty.
Sergeant Chavez joined Zamora at the site and saw the burned brush and ground marks.

official.agency: US Air Force, Project Blue Book
official.note: Investigated the case and classified it as unknown.

sources.title: Project Blue Book: Socorro, New Mexico, April 1964 (National Archives)

name: The Betty and Barney Hill abduction
place: Near Lincoln and Indian Head, White Mountains, New Hampshire, USA
coord_source: Wikipedia: Barney and Betty Hill incident (coordinates of the site marker area on US Route 3)
beings: Barney saw figures in glossy black uniforms at the craft's windows; under later hypnosis the couple described short grey-skinned beings with large heads and large, wrap-around eyes.
witnesses: Two witnesses, married couple Betty and Barney Hill of Portsmouth, New Hampshire.
summary: A couple driving through New Hampshire saw a craft with figures at its windows and later recalled being taken aboard.
body: Late on September 19, 1961, Betty and Barney Hill were driving home to Portsmouth from a holiday in Canada along US Route 3 when Betty noticed a bright light that seemed to move across the sky. They stopped several times to watch it through binoculars. South of Indian Head, they said, the object came down close to their car. Barney walked toward it and said he saw eight to eleven figures in dark uniforms looking out of its windows, one of whom seemed to tell him to stay where he was. Terrified, he ran back to the car and they drove off.

The Hills said they then heard beeping sounds and felt drowsy, and that their memories of the next 35 miles or so of road were patchy. They reached home hours later than expected. Over the following weeks Betty had vivid dreams of being taken aboard a craft, and the couple talked with investigators from the civilian group NICAP. In 1964 they underwent hypnosis with Boston psychiatrist Benjamin Simon, during which both described being taken aboard and examined by short grey beings with large eyes. Simon later wrote that he regarded the case as a singular psychological aberration rather than a literal abduction.

The Hills reported the sighting to Pease Air Force Base, and Project Blue Book has a file under Lincoln, New Hampshire, for that night. Its record card says the visual and radar reports were probably caused by a strong temperature inversion and that the light had the characteristics of an advertising searchlight, and gives no firm identification. Local researcher Jim Macdonald has argued the light was the aircraft warning beacon on Cannon Mountain, with the abduction account shaped by stress, fatigue and hypnosis. Writer Martin Kottmeyer noted that Barney first described the large-eyed beings about two weeks after a similar large-eyed alien appeared on the TV series The Outer Limits.

The Hills' story was published in John G. Fuller's 1966 book The Interrupted Journey and filmed as NBC's 1975 TV movie The UFO Incident. It became the template for later abduction reports. The couple's papers, including the dress Betty wore that night, are held by the University of New Hampshire, and a state historical marker was placed near the site in 2011.
status_note: Blue Book did not identify the light, and the abduction memories rest on hypnosis that skeptics and the Hills' own psychiatrist doubted.

official.agency: US Air Force, Pease Air Force Base
official.note: On a friend's advice, the Hills reported the sighting to Pease AFB.

official.note: File for Lincoln, New Hampshire, September 20, 1961; the card suggests an inversion and searchlight but gives no firm conclusion.

name: The Travis Walton abduction
place: Apache–Sitgreaves National Forests, near Heber, Arizona, USA
coord_source: Wikipedia: Heber–Overgaard, Arizona (nearest town; the Turkey Springs work site is in the forest nearby)
beings: Walton said he woke in a hospital-like room watched by three short, bald humanoids with large eyes, and later met a helmeted, human-looking man.
witnesses: Travis Walton and six other members of a forestry crew led by Mike Rogers.
summary: A logging crew said a glowing craft struck Travis Walton with a beam; he reappeared five days later describing alien captors.
body: On the evening of November 5, 1975, a seven-man forestry crew working at Turkey Springs in the Apache–Sitgreaves National Forests was driving home when, they said, they saw a glowing object hovering near the road. Crew member Travis Walton got out and walked toward it. The others said a beam of light struck him and threw him to the ground, and they drove off in fear. When they came back about 15 minutes later, they said, Walton and the light were gone.

Crew chief Mike Rogers reported Walton missing to the Navajo County sheriff. Searches over the following days, including a helicopter, found no trace of him. On November 11 the six crew members took polygraph tests from the Arizona Department of Public Safety, mainly to rule out foul play; the examiner judged five truthful and one inconclusive. Five days after vanishing, Walton phoned his family from a payphone in Heber. He later said he had woken aboard a craft, fought off three short, bald beings with large eyes, been led away by a human-looking man in a helmet and then blacked out, remembering nothing more until he found himself by a highway.

The case soon became a media story. Walton and his family worked with the National Enquirer, which paid for his stay and awarded the crew a prize after other polygraph tests. Skeptics Philip J. Klass and Michael Shermer argued it was a hoax, noting that an early polygraph found Walton showed "gross deception", that Walton and his family were longtime UFO enthusiasts, and that the crew was behind on a Forest Service contract that a dramatic event might excuse. Investigators later suggested a nearby fire lookout tower could have been used to stage the light.

In 2021 Rogers said in a recorded call that the event had been staged, then retracted the statement; after his death in 2026 his daughter said he had made a deathbed confession. Walton has always maintained the abduction was real. His 1978 book The Walton Experience became the 1993 film Fire in the Sky.
status_note: Walton maintains it happened; a crew member's later hoax confessions were retracted or reported second-hand, so the case is not settled.

official.note: Led the missing-person search for Walton in November 1975.
Gave polygraph tests to the six crew members on November 11, 1975, mainly to rule out foul play.

name: The Ariel School encounter
coord_source: Wikipedia: Ariel School UFO incident (school coordinates)
beings: Children described one to four small figures dressed in black, with large eyes, who came out of a silver craft in the scrub near the playground.
witnesses: Around 62 pupils aged 6 to 12 at Ariel, a private primary school; staff were in a meeting at the time.
summary: Dozens of pupils at a Zimbabwe school said a silver craft landed by the playground and small black-clad beings approached.
body: At about 10 a.m. on September 16, 1994, during morning break at Ariel School near Ruwa, about 22 km southeast of Harare, a large group of children said one or more silver, disc-shaped objects came down into the brush and trees just beyond the school grounds. Teachers were inside at a meeting; the only adult nearby ran the tuck shop. The episode lasted about 15 minutes.

Children said one or more small beings dressed in black, with big eyes, came out and moved toward them. Many ran, while some older pupils stayed to watch. Teachers at first dismissed the reports, but parents came in the next day. Some children thought they had seen tokoloshes, beings from local folklore, rather than aliens. The sighting came two days after a fireball was seen over southern Africa, which skeptic Brian Dunning attributes to the re-entry of a Russian rocket stage.

BBC correspondent Tim Leach filmed interviews at the school on September 19, and local researcher Cynthia Hind interviewed pupils the next day and had them draw what they saw. In November, Harvard psychiatrist John Mack interviewed children, some of whom then described a telepathic warning about harming the environment. Skeptics note that Hind interviewed the children in groups, which risks stories blending together, and that the environmental message first appeared in Mack's later interviews. Other explanations offered include mass hysteria, a prank, a dust devil, or a travelling puppet show.

In a 2023 Netflix documentary series, one former pupil claimed he had started the story as a joke by calling a shiny rock a UFO, but his claim conflicts with his earlier interviews and with other witnesses. Several former pupils, now adults, still say they saw something real. The case features in the 2020 documentary The Phenomenon and the 2022 film Ariel Phenomenon.
status_note: Many former pupils stand by their accounts, while skeptics propose mass hysteria or contamination between interviews.

sources.title: Witness History: The schoolkids who said they saw 'aliens' (BBC World Service)

name: The Westall sighting
place: Westall High School, Clayton South, Melbourne, Victoria, Australia
beings: No beings were reported; witnesses described a round, domed, silvery object, sometimes with small aircraft circling it. It is included here as a landmark mass sighting, not an entity sighting.
witnesses: Hundreds of students and some teachers at Westall High School, plus a few local residents.
summary: Students and teachers at a Melbourne school watched a silvery object descend near the school; no beings were reported.
body: Important caveat: Westall is an object sighting. No witness reported beings or occupants, and it appears in this section only because it is Australia's best-known mass close encounter, often paired with the Ariel School case.

On the morning of April 6, 1966, students and a teacher at Westall High School in Melbourne's south-east saw a flying object they described as round, domed and white, grey or silver. Witnesses said it came down behind a row of trees into an open area called the Grange, south of the school. Some said it landed and took off again; others said it only hovered, and some recalled several small aircraft circling it. Students who ran to the Grange described flattened or burnt circles in the grass, though accounts of the number and appearance of the circles vary.

The next day The Age newspaper suggested a weather balloon released from Laverton. Air force personnel and UFO enthusiasts visited the field on April 9 and reported nothing of interest, and the landowner later burned off the field. Researcher Keith Basterfield found documents suggesting a stray balloon from the HIBAL high-altitude radiation-sampling programme may have come down near the school, which would fit descriptions of a silvery object with a trailing parachute. Skeptic Brian Dunning added that a towed aircraft target could explain the circling planes. Some witnesses later said men in suits told them not to talk about it.

No government records documenting an investigation have been made public, which many witnesses find frustrating. Skeptic Richard Saunders argues that decades of retelling have blended real memories with false ones. The case is the subject of the documentary Westall '66, a 2026 episode of the ABC's Australian Story, anniversary reunions and the City of Kingston's Grange Reserve UFO Park playground.
status_note: A stray research balloon is the leading explanation, but no official record confirms it and witnesses dispute it.

official.note: Air force personnel are reported to have visited the field on April 9, 1966, and found nothing of interest.

sources.title: After 60 years, witnesses to Australia's biggest UFO sighting say it's time for answers (ABC News)

name: The Dover Demon sightings
beings: Witnesses described a thin, hairless figure about 4 feet tall with a large watermelon-shaped head, glowing orange eyes, no visible nose or mouth, and long spindly limbs and fingers.
witnesses: Three teenagers, aged 15 to 17, in three separate sightings over two nights.
summary: Over two nights, three teenagers in Dover, Massachusetts, said they saw a spindly, big-headed creature with glowing eyes.
body: On the night of April 21, 1977, a 17-year-old driving along Farm Street in Dover, a town about 15 miles southwest of Boston, said his headlights picked out a strange figure on a broken stone wall. He described it as about 4 feet tall, with a large head shaped like a watermelon, glowing orange eyes and no visible nose or mouth. Later that night a 15-year-old said he saw a similar creature on Miller Hill Road, and the next night another 15-year-old reported one on Springdale Avenue.

Each teenager made a sketch, and the first witness signed his with a statement that he would swear on a stack of Bibles to what he saw. Plotted on a map, the three sightings fell along a line about two miles long. No UFO was reported, but UFO groups and cryptozoologist Loren Coleman investigated, and the story reached the press in May 1977.

Local police told the Associated Press the reports were probably nothing more than a school vacation hoax, though none of the witnesses ever admitted one. Skeptic Joe Nickell proposed a snowy owl, its partly spread wings looking like spindly arms; others suggested a young moose or foal. Skeptic Brian Dunning doubted the owl idea but still favoured an ordinary explanation. Dunning has said he is not calling the teenagers liars, but regards the story as almost certainly not literally true.
The Dover Demon became one of New England's best-known modern monsters, appearing in TV shows such as Lost Tapes, in several comic books and as a character in the manga and anime Dandadan.
status_note: Police suspected a prank and skeptics suggest an owl or young animal, but no hoax was admitted and nothing was found.

official.note: Told the Associated Press the sightings were probably a school vacation hoax.

sources.title: The Legend of the Dover Demon (Skeptoid #965)

name: The Allagash abductions
place: Eagle Lake, Allagash Wilderness Waterway, Maine, USA
coord_source: Wikipedia: Eagle Lake (Maine), the Allagash Wilderness Waterway lake in Piscataquis County
beings: Under hypnosis the men described thin, spindly beings in body suits with large heads, long necks, large elliptical eyes without lids and four-fingered, insect-like hands.
witnesses: Four men on a canoe trip: twin brothers Jack and Jim Weiner, Chuck Rak and their guide Charlie Foltz.
summary: Four canoeists in the Maine woods saw a glowing sphere; years later, under hypnosis, they described being taken aboard.
body: In August 1976, four young men, three of them art students from Massachusetts and one their guide, were canoeing the Allagash Wilderness Waterway in northern Maine. On the night usually given as August 26, they built a large bonfire on the shore of Eagle Lake and paddled out to fish. They said a huge sphere of coloured light, about 80 feet across, rose over the cove. When the guide signalled at it with a flashlight, it moved toward them and shone a cone-shaped beam on the canoe.

Their next memory, they said, was being back on shore watching the object leave, with the bonfire, which they had expected to burn for hours, reduced to embers. They reported the light to a park ranger, who suggested it was a searchlight from a store opening many miles away.

Years later, after Jack Weiner had suffered nightmares, his twin Jim approached ufologist Raymond Fowler at a conference, and Fowler arranged hypnosis sessions for all four. Under hypnosis they described being taken aboard the craft, examined and sampled by long-necked, large-eyed beings, and they made sketches of them. Fowler's 1993 book The Allagash Abductions presented the case, noting that the men passed polygraph tests. The story was featured on Unsolved Mysteries and other TV shows.

In 2016 Chuck Rak told a Maine newspaper that the abduction never happened. He said they did see an unexplained light, but that the hypnosis did not produce real memories for him, that he had backed the story to make money, and that the group had been smoking marijuana. The other three rejected his account and stand by the story. Critics also point to well-known problems with memories recovered under hypnosis.
status_note: One of the four witnesses has disowned the abduction story, while the other three maintain it.

sources.title: How much of a famed 1976 UFO abduction is true? (The County / Houlton Pioneer Times, 2016)
13 Days of Halloween Tales of Terror: The Allagash Abductions (Boothbay Register)

name: The Cisco Grove encounter
place: Near Cisco Grove, Placer County, California, USA
beings: The hunter described two human-like figures in silvery suits with no visible neck and large, protruding eyes, plus a third, robot-like figure that he said gave off a vapour.
witnesses: One witness, a bow hunter from the Sacramento area, about 27, who had become separated from two companions.
summary: A bow hunter stranded in the Sierra said silver-suited beings and a robot kept him trapped up a pine tree all night.
body: On Friday, September 4, 1964, three men from the Sacramento area went bow hunting in the Sierra Nevada near Cisco Grove, off US Highway 40, and became separated. According to the Air Force summary of the witness's taped interview, one man, alone at dusk, saw lights he took for a helicopter searching for him and lit signal fires on a ridge above Granite Creek. The lights, he said, turned out to be three silvery objects that circled his position and dropped two smaller objects.

Hearing loud crashing in the brush, he climbed into a tall pine. He said two human-like figures in silvery suits, with no visible neck and large protruding eyes, approached and tried to dislodge him, joined by a third figure he called a robot. He fired arrows at the robot and set pieces of his clothing alight and threw them down, which he said made the beings react violently. He said a vapour from the robots made him black out, and that he strapped himself to the tree with his belt. At dawn the craft and the beings were gone, and he rejoined his companions.

His father-in-law urged him to report it. He told an instructor at Sacramento City College's observatory, who notified Mather Air Force Base; intelligence officers from McClellan Air Force Base recorded an interview on September 21 and described him as stable and convinced of his account. The Foreign Technology Division asked whether owls or other animals and an overactive imagination might explain it. Project Blue Book filed the case under "Sacto Area, California" and concluded the encounter with "beings" was psychological. The file notes that the tape and the arrow he fired were kept as specimens.
The case is a staple of UFO literature and has been retold in books and podcasts, but no physical evidence beyond the arrow was ever reported.
status_note: Project Blue Book attributed the encounter to psychological causes; the witness stood by it and nothing else was found.

official.agency: US Air Force, McClellan and Mather Air Force Bases
official.note: Intelligence officers of the 552nd AEW&C Wing interviewed the witness on tape on September 21, 1964.

official.agency: US Air Force, Project Blue Book
official.note: Filed as "Sacto Area, California, 4 September 1964"; conclusion: other (psychological).

name: The Loveland frogmen
beings: The 1955 legend describes three upright figures 3 to 4 feet tall with leathery skin and frog-like faces; the 1972 police sighting was of a leathery animal 3 to 4 feet long that crouched like a frog and briefly stood upright.
witnesses: An unnamed driver in the 1955 story; Loveland police officers Ray Shockey and Mark Matthews in 1972.
summary: Loveland's frog-faced humanoids began as a 1955 roadside tale; a 1972 police sighting was later blamed on an iguana.
body: The Loveland frog legend has two parts. According to later retellings, in 1955 (some versions say May) a businessman driving at night near the Branch Hill area of Loveland saw three figures standing upright by the road, 3 to 4 feet tall, with leathery skin and frog-like faces; some versions add that one held up a wand that threw sparks. No contemporary report of this sighting is known, and details differ between versions.

The better-documented episode came at about 1 a.m. on March 3, 1972. Loveland police officer Ray Shockey said an animal crossed Riverside Drive in his headlights near the Little Miami River. He described it as 3 to 4 feet long, leathery and weighing perhaps 50 to 75 pounds; it crouched like a frog, then stood up to climb over the guardrail and went down toward the river.

About two weeks later a second officer, Mark Matthews, said he saw a similar animal by the road nearby, shot it and found it was a large iguana, about 3 feet long and missing its tail, probably a released pet. He said Shockey confirmed it was the animal he had seen. Matthews has since called the frogman story a hoax and complained that authors left out the iguana. Skeptoid noted it could not find coverage of the 1972 sightings in local papers of the time.

Despite this, the Loveland frog has become a beloved local legend. It inspired the 2014 musical Hot Damn! It's the Loveland Frog!, the 2023 horror film Frogman and the 2023 documentary Finding Frogman, and in 2023 a frog prince costume became the city's mascot. A 2016 report of a frog-like figure by the river, from people playing Pokémon Go, briefly revived the story.
status_note: The 1972 sighting was later attributed to an iguana by an officer involved; the 1955 story is unverified folklore.

official.note: Two on-duty officers described the 1972 sightings; one says he shot the animal and it was an iguana.

sources.title: Officer who shot Loveland Frogman in 1972 says story is a hoax (WCPO)

name: The Antônio Vilas-Boas abduction
place: São Francisco de Sales, Minas Gerais, Brazil
coord_source: Wikipedia: São Francisco de Sales (municipality coordinates)
beings: He described beings about 5 feet tall in tight grey coveralls and helmets with small blue eyes, who spoke in barking sounds, and a small fair-haired woman with large, slanted blue eyes.
witnesses: One witness, 23-year-old farmer Antônio Vilas-Boas.
summary: A young Brazilian farmer said helmeted beings dragged him from his tractor into an egg-shaped craft one night in 1957.
body: On the night of October 15, 1957, Antônio Vilas-Boas, a 23-year-old farmer, was ploughing his family's fields near São Francisco de Sales in Minas Gerais, working at night to avoid the heat. He said a light he took for a red star came closer until it became an egg-shaped craft with a red light at the front and a rotating dome, which landed on three legs. When he tried to drive off, his tractor's engine and lights died.

He said he was seized by a helmeted being about 5 feet tall in grey coveralls, and three others helped drag him aboard. Inside, he said, he was stripped, covered in a gel and had a blood sample taken from his chin, and was made ill by a gas. He then said a small woman with pale hair and slanted blue eyes came in and had sex with him, afterwards pointing to her belly and upward. He was shown around the craft, failed in an attempt to take a device as proof, and watched the craft leave. He said about four hours had passed.

Vilas-Boas later contacted journalist João Martins, who brought in physician Olavo Fontes. Fontes interviewed and examined him in 1958, recorded skin lesions and other symptoms, and believed he had mild radiation sickness. No hypnosis was used. There was no government investigation. The story circulated among researchers for several years before appearing in print in the early 1960s.

Researcher Peter Rogerson doubted the account, noting that a similar story had been printed in the magazine O Cruzeiro a few months before Vilas-Boas first told his own, and that Vilas-Boas, far from being an unworldly peasant, was an ambitious young man taking a correspondence course. Vilas-Boas, who later became a lawyer and raised a family, stood by his story until his death in 1991. It was one of the first modern abduction claims to get wide attention, four years before the Hill case.
status_note: The single-witness account was never independently checked, and skeptics suspect it borrowed from earlier published stories.

name: The Boianai sightings (Father Gill)
place: Boianai Anglican mission, Milne Bay, Papua New Guinea
coord_source: OpenStreetMap: Boianai Anglican Church, Milne Bay Province
beings: Witnesses said one to four human-like figures appeared on the deck of a large, glowing, disc-shaped craft and moved about; on the second evening they appeared to wave back.
witnesses: Anglican missionary Rev. William Gill and more than 30 people at his mission, including teachers and villagers.
summary: An Anglican priest and dozens of mission villagers in Papua watched figures on a hovering craft, which seemed to wave back.
body: On the evening of June 26, 1959, Rev. William Gill, an Australian Anglican priest running the mission at Boianai in what was then the Australian territory of Papua, said he and dozens of mission staff and villagers watched a large, glowing, disc-shaped object hovering over the sea and bay. Gill's notes describe a craft with a wide base, an upper deck and leg-like supports, a blue beam of light angled upward, and smaller lights in the sky over about four hours. On the deck, they said, figures appeared, from one up to four, moving about as if busy with some task.

The following evening the object returned. Gill said that when he and others waved, the figures on the deck waved back. He signalled with a torch, and the object seemed to swing toward them before the figures went below. Gill had previously been skeptical of flying saucer reports.

Gill's report was passed to Australian members of parliament, and a question was raised in the federal parliament. The Royal Australian Air Force interviewed Gill in December 1959, and its officer concluded the lights were probably the planets Jupiter, Saturn and Mars seen through moving cloud. The US Air Force's Project Blue Book also holds a New Guinea file for June–July 1959 describing a bright light with men moving on top, which it put down to misinterpreted astronomical bodies.

Astronomer J. Allen Hynek visited Boianai in 1973 and, with investigator Allan Hendry, accepted that the smaller lights could be stars and planets but argued the large object's size and steadiness ruled that out. Other suggestions include a misjudged Venus or the lights of a fishing boat. Gill did not retract his account, and the case remains one of the most cited close encounters of the third kind.
status_note: The RAAF and Blue Book blamed planets, but Hynek and others argued that cannot explain the main object.

official.note: Interviewed Rev. Gill on December 29, 1959, and concluded the sightings were probably planets seen through cloud.
A question about the sightings was put to the Minister for Air on November 24, 1959.

official.agency: US Air Force, Project Blue Book
official.note: New Guinea file (June–July 1959) concludes misinterpretation of astronomical bodies.

sources.title: Project Blue Book: New Guinea, June 1959 (National Archives)

name: The Eagle River pancakes
place: Eagle River, Vilas County, Wisconsin, USA
beings: Simonton described three clean-shaven, ordinary-looking short men with dark hair, dressed in black, one with a red stripe on his trousers.
witnesses: One witness, local plumber Joe Simonton.
summary: A Wisconsin plumber said three small men in a silver saucer asked for water and gave him pancakes in return.
body: Around 11 a.m. on April 18, 1961, Joe Simonton, a plumber in Eagle River, Wisconsin, said a silvery saucer landed near his house. Three short, dark-haired men dressed in black were aboard, he said, and one held out a jug, which he took as a request for water. He filled it, and in return was handed some small cakes, about three inches across, which he said tasted like cardboard. He said the craft hummed like a generator and took off after about five minutes, its blast bending nearby pine trees.

Simonton gave the cakes to local judge Frank Carter, a member of the civilian UFO group NICAP. The story went out on the wire services on April 23, and the local district attorney and newspaper editor described Simonton as reputable and straightforward. The US Air Force sent its consultant, astronomer J. Allen Hynek, who concluded that Simonton had experienced a hallucination followed by a delusion. A government laboratory analysis reported that a pancake was made of ordinary flour, sugar, salt and oil.

The case split UFO believers. NICAP declined to get involved, fearing ridicule, while writer Jacques Vallée later compared Simonton's story to folklore of fairies offering food and used it to argue against a simple space-visitor explanation. Hynek later said he had come to take Simonton more seriously. Others have suggested Simonton dreamt the encounter or was the butt of a prank.

Simonton, who said he would not report it again if it happened twice, died in 1971. A piece of one of the pancakes is reported to be held by the National Museum of the United States Air Force, and the case is still described as Wisconsin's most famous alien encounter claim.
status_note: The Air Force's investigator called it a hallucination; the witness never changed his story.

official.agency: US Air Force, Project Blue Book
official.note: Investigated through consultant J. Allen Hynek, who concluded hallucination; Blue Book file for Eagle River, April 1961.
Analysed a pancake and found ordinary ingredients, as reported in June 1961.

sources.title: Project Blue Book: Eagle River, Wisconsin, April 1961 (National Archives)

name: The Voronezh landing
coord_source: Wikipedia: Voronezh (city coordinates; the reported landing was in a city park)
beings: Children described one to three very tall figures, about 3 metres high, with small heads, silvery suits and, in some accounts, three eyes, together with a small robot.
witnesses: A group of about ten children aged roughly 12 to 13 playing football in a park, plus some later reports from residents.
summary: Soviet news agency TASS reported children's claims that tall, small-headed beings and a robot left a craft in a Voronezh park.
body: On September 27, 1989, a group of boys playing football in a park in Voronezh, a city about 300 miles south of Moscow, said they saw a pink glow and then a deep red ball about three metres across. They said it landed, and that very tall beings with small heads, along with a small robot, stepped out and walked about. Some accounts add that one being made a teenage boy vanish briefly with a ray gun. A local police lieutenant said he had seen a body flying in the sky.

The official Soviet news agency TASS reported the story on October 9, 1989, saying local scientists had confirmed a landing site and found unusual rock. The report caused a sensation abroad, coming at a time when Soviet state media were publishing many paranormal stories under the new policy of openness.

The claims quickly fell apart under scrutiny. The TASS correspondent told United Press International he had not seen anything himself and that his source was about ten children aged 12 to 13. The head of the local geophysical laboratory said the "alien" rock was ordinary hematite and that the site had been found by dowsing; he told a newspaper not to believe everything TASS reported. A university official said a raised level of caesium at the site was a common legacy of Chernobyl, and later reports said dozens of soil and plant tests found nothing unusual. A Soviet TV crew found no witnesses other than the children.

Skeptics such as Paul Kurtz saw Voronezh as a case of children's imagination amplified by state media. The story briefly made Voronezh a destination for UFO tours, and it remains the best-known Soviet-era entity case.
status_note: Rests on children's accounts amplified by TASS; follow-up tests found no evidence of a landing.

official.note: Reported the landing on October 9, 1989, citing local scientists.
A police lieutenant said he saw a body flying in the sky; the Interior Ministry said troops could be sent if the object returned.

sources.title: Soviet UFO experts doubt nocturnal space visit reported by Tass (UPI, October 11, 1989)

name: The Falcon Lake incident
place: Falcon Lake, Whiteshell Provincial Park, Manitoba, Canada
coord_source: Wikipedia: Falcon Lake, Manitoba (community coordinates; the claimed landing site was in the bush nearby)
beings: No beings were seen. Michalak said he heard voices from inside the landed craft that sounded "definitely human", and he believed the craft was man-made.
witnesses: One witness: Stefan (Steve) Michalak, a 50-year-old Winnipeg industrial mechanic and amateur prospector.
summary: A Winnipeg prospector said a landed craft burned his chest in a grid pattern; CBC has called it Canada's best-documented UFO case.
status_note: Michalak was really burned, but investigators found no landing site at first, his story changed, and later marks were judged self-inflicted.
body: On Saturday, May 20, 1967, at about 3 p.m., Stefan Michalak flagged down an RCMP highway patrol constable on the Trans-Canada Highway near Falcon Beach. He said he had seen two glowing red, rotating "spaceships", that he had touched one, and that it had burned his hat and shirt. He warned the officer not to come close in case he carried radiation. That night he was treated in Winnipeg for first-degree burns.

Michalak told the Winnipeg Tribune that one of the objects landed. He described it as metallic and about 35 feet long, with a door that opened to show violet light, a hissing sound and human-sounding voices. He said he spoke to it in several languages and got no answer, and that when it lifted off, its exhaust burned him in a checkerboard pattern. He reported headaches, vomiting and weight loss afterwards.

The RCMP, the RCAF, the Department of National Defence and the Department of Health all looked into it, and the US Condon Committee reviewed it. A first aerial and ground search failed to find the site. In late June, Michalak said he had gone back with a friend and collected his burnt shirt and soil; one soil sample tested highly radioactive, and he then led officials to a spot where moss had been removed in a semicircle. Only trace radiation was found there, and chemists suggested contamination, for example from radium-based paint.

In January 1968 Michalak showed the press a neat grid of marks on his abdomen and said his burns had come back. A Mayo Clinic psychiatrist judged the new marks to be self-inflicted. Sceptic Aaron Sakulich argued the original burns were most likely an accident, and that the story kept rival prospectors away. Supporters, including Michalak's son, say a blue-collar mechanic could not have invented it. The Royal Canadian Mint put the event on a silver coin in 2018.

official.note: Took the first report on the highway and interviewed Michalak at home; searched the area by air and on foot with the RCAF.

official.agency: Royal Canadian Air Force / Department of National Defence
official.note: Investigated the claim; records are held at Library and Archives Canada.
Tested the soil and items for radiation and found only low, non-dangerous levels at the site.
Reviewed the case as part of its 1966–1968 UFO study.

name: The Langenburg saucers
coord_source: Wikipedia: Langenburg, Saskatchewan (town coordinates; the field was on a farm in the area)
beings: No beings were seen. The farmer described five saucer-shaped objects spinning just above the ground.
witnesses: One witness: Edwin Fuhr, a farmer swathing his crop.
summary: A Saskatchewan farmer said five spinning saucers hovered by a slough; the RCMP found five matching circles in the field.
status_note: The RCMP found the circles and no sign of anyone driving in to make them; no explanation was settled on.
body: At about 10:30 a.m. on September 1, 1974, Edwin Fuhr was swathing a field near Langenburg, Saskatchewan, when he saw five saucer-shaped objects hovering about a foot off the ground near a slough. He first thought it was a prank and walked closer, then saw that the objects were spinning fast.
Fuhr said his swather would not restart, and he sat watching for about 15 minutes, too scared to move. The objects then took off very fast and in silence, leaving only a grey vapour.

The RCMP investigated and found five circles in the field matching Fuhr's description, with no physical sign that anyone had driven in to make them. The Royal Canadian Mint marked the event with a silver coin in 2024.

official.note: Investigated and recorded five circles in the field matching the witness's account.
